One commenter said that if they were a customer they would be angry, but called Checkout.com's breach handling about as good as it gets: a timely response, disclosure by the company itself rather than a third party, an actual expression of shame and remorse, and a decent explanation of the target and scope. They said few breached companies do well on all of these points.

One commenter called the donation to security research virtue signaling. They argued that good protection practices are already well known and just need to be implemented, so the money should have gone into better protections or hiring someone responsible. They noted the hack happened on a legacy system that was not properly decommissioned.

A former fintech worker thought the stolen data was likely merchant KYB onboarding documents. That data is handled very differently from card numbers, which are encrypted using HSMs. They said that if it was only KYB data it does not harm individuals much, since much KYB information is public, and credited Checkout.com for being open about it.

One commenter worried that the leaked onboarding data probably includes director passport and ID scans. They said this creates identity theft risk for years: fraudsters could register with another PSP using the stolen documents, or open bank accounts using the victims' details and tax IDs.

One critic said the apology talks of transparency, accountability and trust but does not publicly explain what happened or what data was taken. They noted there is no promise of further information, and called the statement marketing while affected merchants are contacted and an undisclosed sum is given to a university.

One commenter accused Checkout.com of downplaying the breach. They pointed out that the statement stresses merchant funds and card numbers weren't accessed, yet the company is contacting 'impacted' merchants. In their view this means the stolen onboarding materials likely include identification documents that enable identity theft.

One commenter said that for a core payments infrastructure provider, framing the hack around its virtuous refusal to pay the ransom buries the lede of getting hacked. They called it 'a swing and a miss.'

One commenter said that if they were among the 'less than 25%' of merchants affected, they would not be pleased with the donation. They asked why Checkout.com didn't compensate affected customers instead.
One commenter found Checkout.com's disclosure and refusal to pay the ransom 'incredibly courageous.' They said they will consider becoming a customer in the future.

One commenter supported the move and pushed back on the cynicism in the thread. They argued the company could have kept the breach quiet, and said they appreciate that it came forward and funded academic research whose results everyone benefits from.

One commenter noted that the breached onboarding materials mean attackers have the KYC data on founders, key personnel and the corporation, enough to impersonate business accounts. They added 'Yikes,' since it affects up to 25% of the current merchant base.
One commenter felt the 'third-party' wording about the hacked legacy cloud storage system reads like an attempt to shift part of the blame onto the storage provider.
